desc:
A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes in which every two neighbours in the sequence are connected by an edge (parent and child), and no node appears twice. A path may start and end at any nodes, does not have to pass through the root, and can go up to a common ancestor and then down again. It must contain at least one node.

The sum of a path is the sum of its node values, which can be negative. Return the largest path sum over all paths.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). Node values can be negative in this problem, so a missing child is written as 1000 (real node values always lie between -500 and 500, so the marker can never be confused with a value). The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing 1000 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with 1000. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, 1000, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [-10, 9, 20, 1000, 1000, 15, 7] the answer is 42, from the path 15 → 20 → 7. For tree = [-3] the answer is -3, because a path needs at least one node.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, missing child written as 1000, no trailing 1000)
hints: Look at the highest node of the best path (where it turns). A path that peaks at v is made of v plus a downward chain on the left plus a downward chain on the right.
For each node define down[v]: the best sum of a downward chain that starts at v. A child's chain is only worth taking if it is positive; otherwise skip it.

down[v] = val[v] + max(0, down[left], down[right]), and the best path peaking at v is val[v] + max(0, down[left]) + max(0, down[right]). The answer is the maximum of the latter over all nodes (it can be negative, so start from -infinity).
editorial: Every path has exactly one highest node, so classify the paths by this peak. For a path peaking at v, the part below v on each side is a downward chain starting at a child, or nothing at all. Both sides are independent, so the best choice on each side is the best downward chain from the child, or 0 (take nothing) if every chain is negative.

Let down[v] be the best sum of a downward chain that starts at v and contains at least v. Then down[v] = val[v] + max(0, down[left], down[right]) because the chain either stops at v or continues into exactly one child. The best path with peak v is val[v] + max(0, down[left]) + max(0, down[right]), and the answer is the maximum of this over all nodes.

Pitfalls: initialising the answer with 0 is wrong when every value is negative (the path must have a node), and returning the two-sided sum from a node to its parent would let a path fork. A backwards pass over the level-order array processes children before parents, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.
